chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter grows out of one question: why do some resized copies of a picture look right and others look stretched? The answer, that both measurements change by the same factor, becomes the idea of a ratio and of two ratios being proportional, and every later problem (recipes, wages, speeds, prices, sharing, units) is first tested for proportionality before it is scaled.

points.title: Predict, then test the factor
points.text: Every concept opens with a prediction, such as which coffee is stronger or how much rice a cook needs, and the factor of change or the simplest form then settles it.

points.title: Multiply, do not add
points.text: Adding the same number to both terms (ages, picture sides) is set against multiplying both terms by the same factor, so students learn to ask which change keeps the ratio.

points.title: Check before you scale
points.text: Speed and time, and the prices of different shampoo bottles, show that not every pair of quantities is proportional; the Rule of Three is used only after that check.

points.title: Tools only where handling is the idea
points.text: Nine tools, each used once: stretching a picture, mixing two drinks, filling a ratio table, a double number line, judging additive or multiplicative change, finding a unit rate, sharing a bar in a ratio, matching temperatures, and bridging units.

content.text:
You may notice that images A, C, and D are rectangular, but E is square. Maybe that is why E looks different. But B is also a rectangle! Why does it look different from the other rectangular images?
Can we observe any pattern to answer this question? Perhaps by measuring the rectangles?
Image A: width 60 mm, height 40 mm. Image B: width 40 mm, height 20 mm. Image C: width 30 mm, height 20 mm. Image D: width 90 mm, height 60 mm. Image E: width 60 mm, height 60 mm.
What makes images A, C, and D appear similar, and B and E different?
When we compare image A with C, we notice that the width of C is half that of A. The height is also half of A. Both the width and height have changed by the same factor (through multiplication), 1/2 in this case. Since the widths and heights have changed by the same factor, the images look similar.
When we compare image A with image B, we notice that the width of B is 20 millimetre (mm) less than that of A. The height too is 20 mm less than the height of A. Even though the difference (through subtraction) is the same, the images look different. Have the width and height changed by the same factor? The height of B is half the height of A. But the width of B is not half the width of A. Since the width and height have not changed by the same factor, the images look different.

1. Predict first: image B is 20 mm narrower and 20 mm shorter than image A. Should it look like A?
2. Measure: A is 60 mm by 40 mm, B is 40 mm by 20 mm, C is 30 mm by 20 mm.

4. From A to B, both sides lose 20 mm, the same difference, but the height is halved while the width is not, so B looks stretched.

content.text:
Worked example: Image A is 60 mm wide and 40 mm high. Image C is 30 mm by 20 mm and image B is 40 mm by 20 mm. Which of B and C changed both sides by the same factor?
1. A to C: 60 ÷ 2 = 30 and 40 ÷ 2 = 20, so both sides are multiplied by 1/2.
2. A to B: 60 − 20 = 40 and 40 − 20 = 20, so both sides lose the same 20 mm.
3. But for B the height factor is 20 ÷ 40 = 1/2, while the width factor is 40 ÷ 60 = 2/3.
4. The factors are different, so B is stretched; C used one factor, so it keeps the shape.
Answer: C changed both sides by the factor 1/2, so it looks similar to A; B did not

content.text:
Worked example: Image A is 60 mm by 40 mm. Image D is 90 mm by 60 mm and image E is 60 mm by 60 mm. Which of them changed proportionally?
1. D: width factor 90 ÷ 60 = 3/2 and height factor 60 ÷ 40 = 3/2.
2. The two factors are the same, so D is A enlarged by 3/2.
3. E: width factor 60 ÷ 60 = 1 but height factor 60 ÷ 40 = 3/2.
4. The factors differ, so E is not proportional to A.
Answer: D is proportional to A (factor 3/2 on both sides); E is not

media.context: CBSE Class 8, Ganita Prakash Part 1, Chapter 7 Proportional Reasoning, section 7.1 Observing Similarity in Change. This tool OPENS the chapter: it is read before ratio notation is formalised in 7.2 and long before the term scale factor arrives in Part 2, so the controls are named Width factor and Height factor and the condition is stated as 'both sides multiplied by the same factor'. The textbook's own hook is a set of resized digital images, where dragging a corner keeps the picture and pulling one side elongates it; this mount is that hook made testable.

overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Shape is decided by the ratio between the sides, not by their lengths. Multiplying both sides by the same factor leaves that ratio untouched, because the factor cancels. Multiplying by different factors changes the ratio, and adding a constant changes it too, since a constant is a different proportion of a short side than of a long one. conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with the figure at its original size and the indicator HIDDEN, and asks whether doubling the width alone keeps the shape. Beat 2 moves the width slider alone and the figure visibly distorts while the side ratios separate on screen. Beat 3 moves both sliders together and the shape returns, so the condition is read off the ratios rather than off the picture. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setWidthScale, setHeightScale, lockSliders and say. No drag: the agent sets a slider by value.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the figure at its original size with both factors at 1 and the shape indicator hidden, and ask the class to say out loud whether doubling the width alone keeps the shape. Commit the class answer on the prediction pad. Targets: width factor 1, height factor 1. Never move a slider before the prediction is committed and never show the indicator at this call. Call 2. Set the width factor to 2 with the height factor left at 1, and point at the two side ratios as they part. Targets: width factor 2, height factor 1. Read both ratios from the tool's own readout and never from this plan. Call 3. Set the height factor to 2 as well so the two factors agree, and point at the shape indicator as it comes back on. Targets: width factor 2, height factor 2. State the condition only after the indicator has turned on.

hunts: EQUAL FACTOR HUNT: find three pairs of factors that keep the shape and three that do not, then say what the passing pairs share.
SHRINK TEST: find a common factor below 1 and say whether the indicator behaves any differently from an enlargement.
ADDING TRAP: find the one kind of figure whose shape survives adding the same amount to both sides.
NEAR MISS: move one slider by the smallest step you can and find where the indicator goes off.

media.description: A rectangle stands on a unit grid with its original outline held behind it as a faint ghost, and BOTH of the tests the textbook uses are printed and separately labelled: the factor of change on each side (new divided by old, written as a fraction with its decimal beside it) and the width : height ratio in simplest form, before and after. They are different numbers, and mixing them is the commonest way this topic is taught wrongly. Three refutations are drawn rather than asserted. A same-shape ray runs from the origin through the original's far corner, and the scaled figure's corner sits on it exactly when the shape survives - inward as well as outward, so a common factor below one lands on it too. An inscribed circle becomes an obvious oval the moment the two factors part. An additive control grows both sides by the same LENGTH and visibly walks the corner off the ray, which is the additive reading of enlargement refuted rather than merely excluded. The shape indicator is computed from the two factors and never from the slider lock, so locking cannot fake a preserved shape, and a near miss such as 2 against 2.1 turns it off with the factor gap and the tolerance of 0.05 both on screen, so how close is not close enough is a stated threshold rather than a hidden one.

concept.notation: A scale factor multiplies a length. Two figures have the same shape when every pair of matching sides is in the same ratio.
concept.statement: A figure keeps its shape when width and height are multiplied by the same factor. Multiplying by different factors stretches it, and adding the same amount to each side does not preserve shape either, because adding changes the ratio between the sides.
prerequisites: reading a scale factor as a multiplier
misconceptions: Enlargement understood as adding a fixed amount to each side rather than multiplying.
Shape assumed preserved under any stretch, so a wider figure is still called the same shape.
concept.why_it_is_true: Shape is decided by the ratio between the sides, not by their lengths. Multiplying both sides by the same factor leaves that ratio untouched, because the factor cancels. Multiplying by different factors changes the ratio, and adding a constant changes it too, since a constant is a different proportion of a short side than of a long one.
worked_numbers: A 3 by 5 figure scaled by 2 in both directions becomes 6 by 10, and both ratios read 3 to 5.
Scaled by 2 in width only it becomes 6 by 5, and the ratio moves from 3 to 5 to 6 to 5.
Adding 2 to each side gives 5 by 7, whose ratio is 5 to 7 and not 3 to 5.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 states the idea with the case that works: a 3 by 5 figure with both factors at 2 becomes 6 by 10, the corner lands on the ray, and the width : height ratio reads 3 : 5 both before and after. Ask the class out loud, BEFORE reading the screen, whether doubling the width alone would do the same - the guess is what makes beat 2 worth watching.

Beat 2 is the mechanism. The width factor alone moves to 2 and the height factor stays at 1, so the ratio walks from 3 : 5 to 6 : 5, the inscribed circle becomes an oval and the corner leaves the ray by a stated number of grid units. Point at the two factor chips as they part; the picture and the numbers are saying the same thing at the same moment.

Beat 3 closes the commonest gap: the condition says EQUAL, not LARGER. Both factors go to one half, the figure shrinks to 1.5 by 2.5, the corner lands back on the ray between the origin and the original corner, and the indicator comes back on. Never say a doubled figure is 'twice as big' - each side is twice as long, and it covers four grid squares for every one.

content.text:
Figure it Out (ratios and proportions, question 5): Look at the given rectangle. Can you draw a smaller rectangle and a bigger rectangle with the same width to height ratio in your notebooks? Compare your rectangles with your classmates' drawings. Are all of them the same? If they are different from yours, can you think why? Are they wrong?
1. Measure the rectangle and write width : height, for example 6 cm : 4 cm, which is 3 : 2.
2. For a smaller one, multiply both sides by one factor less than 1: 6 × 1/2 = 3 and 4 × 1/2 = 2.
3. For a bigger one, multiply both sides by one factor more than 1: 6 × 2 = 12 and 4 × 2 = 8.
4. Classmates may use other factors, so the sizes differ, but every drawing with ratio 3 : 2 is correct.
Answer: Yes; drawings of different sizes are all correct as long as their width to height ratio is the same

content.text:
Figure it Out (ratios and proportions, question 7): Let us draw some human figures. Measure your friend's body: the lengths of their head, torso, arms and legs. Write the ratios head : torso, torso : arms and torso : legs. Now draw a figure with head, torso, arms and legs in equivalent ratios. Does the drawing look more realistic if the ratios are proportional? Why? Why not?
1. Measure the four lengths, for example head 20 cm, torso 60 cm, arms 60 cm, legs 80 cm.
2. Write the ratios: head : torso is 20 : 60, which is 1 : 3; torso : legs is 60 : 80, which is 3 : 4.
3. Choose one factor for the drawing, for example 1/10: 20 × 1/10 = 2 cm for the head and 60 × 1/10 = 6 cm for the torso.
4. Scaling every length by the same factor keeps the ratios, so the figure looks realistic.
Answer: Yes; when every length is scaled by the same factor, the ratios stay the same and the figure looks realistic

By what factor should we multiply the ratio 60 : 40 (image A) to get 90 : 60 (image D)?
A more systematic way to compare whether the ratios are proportional is to reduce them to their simplest form and see if these simplest forms are the same.
We can reduce ratios to their simplest form by dividing the terms by their HCF.
In image A, the terms are 60 and 40. What is the HCF of 60 and 40? It is 20. Dividing the terms by 20, we get the ratio of image A to be 3 : 2 in its simplest form.
The ratio of image D is 90 : 60. Dividing both terms by 30 (HCF of 90 and 60), we get the simplest form to be 3 : 2. So the ratios of images A and D are proportional as well.
What is the simplest form of the ratios of images B and E?
The ratio of image B is 40 : 20; in its simplest form, it is 2 : 1.
The ratio of image E is 60 : 60; in its simplest form, it is 1 : 1.
These ratios are not the same as 3 : 2. So, we can say that the ratios of width to height of images B and E are not proportional to the ratios of images A, C, and D.
When two ratios are the same in their simplest forms, we say that the ratios are in proportion, or that the ratios are proportional. We use the '::' symbol to indicate that they are proportional.
So a : b :: c : d indicates that the ratios a : b and c : d are proportional.
Thus, 60 : 40 :: 30 : 20 and 60 : 40 :: 90 : 60.

overview.concept: A mixture is decided by the ratio of its two parts and not by their totals. Multiplying both parts by the same number keeps the ratio and therefore the taste. Adding the same amount to both changes the ratio, because the same amount is a different share of a small part than of a large one, so the taste changes.

overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.

overview.neverRemove: Do not show the reduced ratios while a prediction is still open, and never derive a swatch from the totals. A swatch that follows volume would destroy the entire contrast.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Doubling both parts doubles the whole, so each part keeps the same share of the mixture and the shade cannot move. Adding one to each keeps the difference between the parts but changes their ratio, because a fixed amount is proportionally larger for the smaller part. The swatch is computed from the ratio alone, which is why it exposes the difference immediately. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on two matching glasses at the same mixture with both swatches shown and no reduced ratios printed, and ask the class to say out loud whether adding one spoon of concentrate and one spoon of water to the right glass keeps the taste. media.description: Two glasses stand on one counter, each drawn as a stack of unit blocks with the concentrate always at the bottom and always in the same colour, and above them a single taste bar split into two halves that TOUCH. The colour of each half is computed from that glass's reduced ratio alone and never from its totals, so two glasses of different sizes holding the same mixture paint one unbroken colour and the seam between the halves simply disappears; the moment the two mixtures differ, a seam appears across the bar. Adding one block to each part of a glass is always allowed, and it opens that seam while the difference between the parts is still 1, which is the additive strategy failing in front of the class. Multiplying both parts holds the colour perfectly still while the stack visibly grows. Every comparison is settled on exact integers by cross multiplication, so a very close but unequal mixture is reported as different rather than as near enough, and the chapter's own factor of change is printed beside the simplest forms. A glass with no concentrate is a real mixture drawn as plain water; a glass with no water is refused, with the reason on screen.

concept.notation: A mixture is written as concentrate to water, for example 2 to 3. Two mixtures taste the same when their ratios are equivalent.
concept.statement: A mixture is decided by the ratio of its two parts and not by their totals. Multiplying both parts by the same number keeps the ratio and therefore the taste. Adding the same amount to both changes the ratio, because the same amount is a different share of a small part than of a large one, so the taste changes.
misconceptions: The additive strategy applied to a proportional situation, so adding one to each part is expected to keep the mixture.
Judging a mixture by its total volume rather than by the ratio of its parts.
concept.why_it_is_true: Doubling both parts doubles the whole, so each part keeps the same share of the mixture and the shade cannot move. Adding one to each keeps the difference between the parts but changes their ratio, because a fixed amount is proportionally larger for the smaller part. The swatch is computed from the ratio alone, which is why it exposes the difference immediately.
worked_numbers: 2 concentrate to 3 water doubled is 4 to 6, and the shades match.
2 to 3 with one added to each is 3 to 4, and the shade is visibly stronger.
4 to 6 reduces to 2 to 3, so a bigger glass can hold the same mixture.
